messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir's eyes would often scan the room, his gaze darting from one face to another, searching for potential threats. It was a habit he'd developed over the past year, ever since the night his wife, Fatima, had attacked him in their home. The physical abuse had left him with more than just bruises - it had shattered his sense of trust and security. The event itself was still etched vividly in his mind. He remembered the darkness of the room, the sound of Fatima's voice raised in anger, and the feeling of being trapped and helpless. Even now, when he found himself in dark spaces or walked through certain physical locations that reminded him of their home, Amir would feel a wave of anxiety wash over him. The memories came flooding back without warning - the sound of Fatima's screams, the feeling of her hands around his throat. To cope with these triggers, Amir had started to avoid places that reminded him of the event, including their old neighborhood and even certain restaurants they used to frequent. He'd also become hypervigilant towards people, always on the lookout for potential dangers. This constant state of alertness was exhausting, but Amir felt it was necessary - after all, he had been betrayed by someone he trusted. The sound of helicopters or aircraft overhead would also send him spiraling back to that night. He remembered hearing a helicopter flying low over their neighborhood during the attack, and now the sound would instantly transport him back to that moment. When this happened, Amir's mind would fill with disconnected pieces of memories - fragmented images and sounds that didn't quite fit together. Amir had also started wearing concealing clothing, hoping to avoid drawing attention to himself. He felt like he was walking around with a neon sign on his head, advertising his vulnerability to the world. This sense of shame and self-blame was suffocating him - Amir had come to believe that the event happened because of some flaw in his own character. As a community organizer, Amir's work required him to be out in public, meeting new people and building relationships. But since the attack, he'd found it increasingly difficult to connect with others. He felt like he was living in a constant state of fear, always looking over his shoulder, waiting for the next shoe to drop. Fatima had left him shortly after the attack, but Amir's sense of betrayal lingered. He couldn't shake the feeling that he'd somehow deserved what happened to him - that it was all because of who he was as a person. This shattered his long-held beliefs about the world being a just and fair place. It wasn't until Amir started noticing the toll this was taking on his relationships with friends and family that he realized he needed help. His wife, Fatima's sister, had been trying to get him to see a therapist for months, but Amir had resisted. Now, as he sat in his small apartment, surrounded by reminders of a life he used to know, he knew it was time to confront the demons that haunted him. Amir's biggest fear was that he'd never be able to escape the memories of that night - that they'd continue to haunt him forever. But what frightened him most was losing himself completely in this sea of anxiety and self-doubt. He hoped that with therapy, he could begin to rebuild his shattered sense of self and find a way to live without being constantly terrorized by his own memories.
